items.title: CVE-2026-120382: Critical Synology DSM OAuth Flaw Enables Arbitrary File Access
items.summary: Synology has disclosed a critical vulnerability affecting DiskStation Manager (DSM) and BeeStation OS that can allow unauthenticated remote attackers to read or write arbitrary files and trigger denial-of-service conditions. Tracked as CVE-2026-120382, the flaw resides in the OAuth API and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical . The vulnerability is classified as CWE-88: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command . According to Synology, the affected OAuth API fails to properly neutralize command argument delimiters, allowing attacker-controlled input to alter how a downstream command interprets its parameters. No authentication or user interaction is required. The issue is particularly serious for organizations exposing Synology NAS management services to untrusted networks. Successful exploitation could expose confidential files stored on the NAS, allow attackers to modify or replace files, or disrupt device availability. Synology’s official advisory does not currently state that the vulnerability directly enables arbitrary command execution or remote code execution, so the confirmed impact should be limited to the vendor-documented file read/write and denial-of-service capabilities. Contact Sales The vulnerability affects multiple DSM generations as well as BeeStation OS 1.5. Synology recommends updating supported installations as soon as fixed builds become available and deactivating the OAuth Service package as an immediate workaround. As of November 20, 2026, the advisory remains marked Ongoing , with fixes for several affected product branches still in progress. Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize emerging vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-120382 by correlating suspicious access to Synology authentication and OAuth functionality with unexpected file-system activity, unusual DSM service behavior, repeated service failures, and anomalous outbound connections from NAS devices. CVE-2026-120382 analysis CVE-2026-120382 affects Synology DiskStation Manager releases across several major branches. Synology’s detailed advisory lists vulnerable versions before DSM 6.2.4-25556-9, 7.1.1-42962-10, 7.2.1-69057-14, 7.2.2-72806-11, 7.3.2-86009-6, and 7.4.1-90080-2. The current product matrix specifically marks the following supported products as affected: Product Status Fixed release / recommendation BeeStation OS 1.5 Critical Fix ongoing DSM 7.4 Critical Upgrade to 7.4.1-90080-2 or later DSM 7.3 Critical Upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later DSM 7.2.2 Critical Fix ongoing; upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6+ recommended DSM 7.2.1 Critical Fix ongoing; upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6+ recommended DSM 7.1 Critical Fix ongoing APM 1.2 / 2.0 Not affected No action for this CVE DSM Enterprise 1.0 Not affected No action for this CVE SRM 1.2 / 1.3 Not affected No action for this CVE An important detail is that DSM 6.2 does not appear in Synology’s current affected-products table, but the technical version description explicitly identifies versions before DSM 6.2.4-25556-9 as vulnerable. Organizations maintaining older or end-of-life NAS systems should therefore verify the installed build instead of assuming that absence from the current support matrix means the system is safe. The root cause involves improper handling of command argument delimiters inside the OAuth API. Argument injection differs from traditional OS command injection: rather than necessarily inserting an entirely new shell command, an attacker manipulates the arguments supplied to a legitimate backend command so it performs operations that were not intended by the application. Synology has not publicly disclosed the vulnerable function, exact HTTP request format, affected OAuth endpoint, backend command, or the characters required to trigger the flaw. This is consistent with the company’s stated policy of limiting detailed vulnerability information until customers have access to fixes. The CVSS vector is: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H This means exploitation is network-accessible, has low attack complexity, requires no privileges, and does not require victim interaction. Successful attacks can have a high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Arbitrary file read capability is especially significant on a NAS platform because these systems frequently store backups, business documents, credentials, configuration files, and other sensitive data. Depending on the permissions of the vulnerable service, attackers may be able to retrieve data that would normally require authenticated access. Arbitrary file write capability introduces an additional integrity risk. An attacker may potentially overwrite existing data or create files at locations accessible to the vulnerable process. However, neither Synology nor the two supplied reports demonstrate a reliable path from this primitive to direct code execution, so CVE-2026-120382 should not currently be described as a confirmed RCE vulnerability. Attackers could also use the vulnerability to disrupt availability. Synology explicitly lists denial-of-service as an impact, which could make the NAS or affected services temporarily unavailable and interfere with business operations, file sharing, backups, or applications depending on the device. The OAuth Service is particularly important from an exposure perspective because OAuth functionality is intended to support authentication and authorization between applications and Synology services. Synology’s immediate workaround is therefore to deactivate the OAuth Service package , removing the vulnerable functionality from active use until a permanent update is installed. The CVE-2026-120382 PoC status remains favorable to defenders at the time of writing. Neither Synology, CyberPress, nor GBHackers reports a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit, and no independently verified public exploit has been identified as of November 20, 2026. There is likewise no confirmed evidence that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild. Synology’s advisory does not describe active attacks, threat actors, exploitation telemetry, or a known campaign associated with the flaw. This is notably different from several other recent Synology vulnerabilities that have been linked to real-world ransomware or intrusion activity. The absence of observed exploitation should not reduce patching priority. A remotely reachable, unauthenticated file read/write vulnerability with low attack complexity and a 9.8 CVSS score is an attractive target, particularly now that the existence and affected product range are public. For CVE-2026-120382 detection, defenders should monitor Synology management interfaces for unusual unauthenticated requests, unexpected OAuth-related activity, abnormal HTTP request parameters, repeated request failures, and unexpected file-system operations occurring shortly after inbound network activity. On organizations that centrally collect NAS telemetry, useful behavioral signals include unexpected creation or modification of configuration files, changes to application directories, suspicious access to sensitive files, unusual service restarts, and unexplained resource exhaustion or service availability problems. Network telemetry can provide additional context. Security teams should investigate unusual connections to exposed Synology NAS interfaces from unfamiliar external addresses, particularly where the same source generates repeated requests immediately before unexpected file modifications or service instability. Because the flaw is remotely exploitable without credentials, defenders should not restrict hunting to successful DSM logins. A malicious request may reach the vulnerable OAuth functionality without creating the authentication events normally associated with legitimate administrative activity. Organizations should also audit internet exposure. NAS management interfaces generally should not be directly accessible from the public internet unless operational requirements demand it. VPN access, private management networks, IP allowlisting, and reverse-proxy controls can materially reduce the attack surface while permanent updates are being deployed. Traditional CVE-2026-120382 IOCs are currently unavailable. Synology has not published malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, request signatures, or attacker infrastructure associated with the vulnerability because no campaign has been publicly linked to exploitation. This makes behavior-based detection and asset exposure management more valuable than static IOC matching. Security teams should identify vulnerable devices first, determine whether the OAuth Service is active, establish whether the NAS is reachable from untrusted networks, and then investigate anomalies that could indicate probing or exploitation. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on November 19, 2026 , when Synology published advisory Synology-SA-26:21. The advisory was updated only minutes later and remains in Ongoing status. Synology has not disclosed the original vulnerability discovery date or publicly credited a specific researcher in the advisory. The CyberPress and GBHackers reports also cover CVE-2026-123007, an unrelated NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerability affecting some of the same Synology platforms. Administrators should not confuse the two flaws: disabling OAuth addresses the immediate exposure for this vulnerability, while CVE-2026-123007 requires separate remediation such as disabling HTTP/2 or installing the corresponding fixed build. Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-120382 should monitor Synology-SA-26:21 because fix availability remains dynamic across DSM and BeeStation OS branches. The vendor advisory should take precedence over third-party vulnerability databases when determining whether a particular NAS build has received a supported fix. CVE-2026-120382 Mitigation The preferred remediation is to upgrade affected Synology systems to a fixed DSM version as soon as the appropriate package is available. Synology identifies: DSM 7.4: upgrade to 7.4.1-90080-2 or later. DSM 7.3: upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later. DSM 7.2.2 and 7.2.1: Synology recommends moving to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later. DSM 7.1: remediation remains listed as ongoing. BeeStation OS 1.5: remediation remains listed as ongoing. As of the latest advisory revision available on November 20, the DSM 7.3 and 7.4 fixed builds are described as scheduled for release by November 20 rather than confirmed universally available across every device and region. Administrators should therefore verify availability through the Synology Update & Restore interface or Download Center rather than assuming the update has already reached their NAS. If an update is not yet available, Synology’s official temporary workaround is straightforward: Deactivate the OAuth Service package. This mitigation should remain in place until the device has been updated to a version containing the fix. Administrators should first determine whether legitimate applications rely on OAuth functionality. Disabling the package may interrupt integrations that use it for authorization, but the operational impact should be balanced against a remotely exploitable vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS score. Organizations should also restrict management interfaces from unnecessary internet exposure. Place NAS administration behind a VPN or dedicated management network and use firewall rules to limit connections to trusted administrators and systems. Where possible, security teams should block direct inbound access to NAS management services from the internet. This does not replace the vendor patch because an attacker with access to the internal network could still target a vulnerable system, but it substantially reduces exposure to opportunistic scanning. After applying the update, verify the installed DSM build rather than assuming an automatic-update notification confirms remediation. Synology notes that updates may become available at different times depending on region, model, and system configuration. Devices running older DSM branches deserve additional attention. The technical advisory indicates that DSM versions before 6.2.4-25556-9 are affected, while modern remediation guidance centers primarily on supported 7.x releases. Organizations that cannot move an older appliance to a supported secure release should consider replacing, isolating, or removing that system from untrusted networks. Security teams should also inspect systems that were publicly accessible before remediation. Review OAuth-related logs, administrative activity, file changes, service restarts, and unusual network events for evidence that exploitation attempts occurred before the update or workaround was applied. Because arbitrary file writes are part of the confirmed impact, unexplained modification of configuration or application files should be treated more seriously than a normal failed authentication attempt. If suspicious file changes are identified, organizations should assess the NAS as potentially compromised rather than simply restoring the modified files. Important data stored on NAS appliances should be protected by independent backups that attackers cannot modify through the same management plane. Maintaining offline, immutable, or separately authenticated backup copies can limit the operational impact of NAS compromise. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-120382 and how does it work? CVE-2026-120382 is a critical argument-delimiter injection vulnerability in the OAuth API used by Synology DiskStation Manager. Improper neutralization of command arguments can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to influence a backend command and gain the ability to read or write arbitrary files or cause denial of service. Synology classifies the weakness as CWE-88 and assigns it a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8. When was CVE-2026-120382 first discovered? Synology has not publicly disclosed the original discovery date or named a researcher in the current advisory. The vulnerability became public on November 19, 2026, when Synology published Synology-SA-26:21. The advisory was last updated minutes after its initial publication and remains marked Ongoing while fixes for several affected branches are still being prepared. What is the impact of CVE-2026-120382 on systems? Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to read arbitrary files, write arbitrary files, and trigger denial-of-service conditions on affected Synology systems. This could expose sensitive NAS data, allow unauthorized modification of stored files, or disrupt services. Synology has not stated that the vulnerability directly provides arbitrary command execution or RCE. Can CVE-2026-120382 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems running affected DSM builds or BeeStation OS 1.5 remain exposed until the appropriate security update is installed or the OAuth Service is deactivated. The advisory includes affected DSM branches from 6.2 through 7.4, although current support and patch availability differ by release. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-120382? Install the relevant Synology security update as soon as it becomes available. DSM 7.4 systems should move to 7.4.1-90080-2 or later, while DSM 7.3 systems should move to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later. If the update is not yet available, deactivate the OAuth Service package, restrict NAS administration to trusted networks, and avoid exposing management interfaces directly to the internet.

Synology’s advisory does not describe active attacks, threat actors, exploitation telemetry, or a known campaign associated with the flaw. This is notably different from several other recent Synology vulnerabilities that have been linked to real-world ransomware or intrusion activity.

The absence of observed exploitation should not reduce patching priority. A remotely reachable, unauthenticated file read/write vulnerability with low attack complexity and a 9.8 CVSS score is an attractive target, particularly now that the existence and affected product range are public.

For CVE-2026-120382 detection, defenders should monitor Synology management interfaces for unusual unauthenticated requests, unexpected OAuth-related activity, abnormal HTTP request parameters, repeated request failures, and unexpected file-system operations occurring shortly after inbound network activity.

On organizations that centrally collect NAS telemetry, useful behavioral signals include unexpected creation or modification of configuration files, changes to application directories, suspicious access to sensitive files, unusual service restarts, and unexplained resource exhaustion or service availability problems.

Network telemetry can provide additional context. Security teams should investigate unusual connections to exposed Synology NAS interfaces from unfamiliar external addresses, particularly where the same source generates repeated requests immediately before unexpected file modifications or service instability.

Because the flaw is remotely exploitable without credentials, defenders should not restrict hunting to successful DSM logins. A malicious request may reach the vulnerable OAuth functionality without creating the authentication events normally associated with legitimate administrative activity.

Organizations should also audit internet exposure. NAS management interfaces generally should not be directly accessible from the public internet unless operational requirements demand it. VPN access, private management networks, IP allowlisting, and reverse-proxy controls can materially reduce the attack surface while permanent updates are being deployed.

Traditional CVE-2026-120382 IOCs are currently unavailable. Synology has not published malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, request signatures, or attacker infrastructure associated with the vulnerability because no campaign has been publicly linked to exploitation.

This makes behavior-based detection and asset exposure management more valuable than static IOC matching. Security teams should identify vulnerable devices first, determine whether the OAuth Service is active, establish whether the NAS is reachable from untrusted networks, and then investigate anomalies that could indicate probing or exploitation.

The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on November 19, 2026, when Synology published advisory Synology-SA-26:21. The advisory was updated only minutes later and remains in Ongoing status. Synology has not disclosed the original vulnerability discovery date or publicly credited a specific researcher in the advisory.

The CyberPress and GBHackers reports also cover CVE-2026-123007, an unrelated NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerability affecting some of the same Synology platforms. Administrators should not confuse the two flaws: disabling OAuth addresses the immediate exposure for this vulnerability, while CVE-2026-123007 requires separate remediation such as disabling HTTP/2 or installing the corresponding fixed build.

Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-120382 should monitor Synology-SA-26:21 because fix availability remains dynamic across DSM and BeeStation OS branches. The vendor advisory should take precedence over third-party vulnerability databases when determining whether a particular NAS build has received a supported fix.

CVE-2026-120382 Mitigation

The preferred remediation is to upgrade affected Synology systems to a fixed DSM version as soon as the appropriate package is available.

Synology identifies:

  • DSM 7.4: upgrade to 7.4.1-90080-2 or later.
  • DSM 7.3: upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later.
  • DSM 7.2.2 and 7.2.1: Synology recommends moving to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later.
  • DSM 7.1: remediation remains listed as ongoing.
  • BeeStation OS 1.5: remediation remains listed as ongoing.

As of the latest advisory revision available on November 20, the DSM 7.3 and 7.4 fixed builds are described as scheduled for release by November 20 rather than confirmed universally available across every device and region. Administrators should therefore verify availability through the Synology Update & Restore interface or Download Center rather than assuming the update has already reached their NAS.

If an update is not yet available, Synology’s official temporary workaround is straightforward:

Deactivate the OAuth Service package.

This mitigation should remain in place until the device has been updated to a version containing the fix.

Administrators should first determine whether legitimate applications rely on OAuth functionality. Disabling the package may interrupt integrations that use it for authorization, but the operational impact should be balanced against a remotely exploitable vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS score.

Organizations should also restrict management interfaces from unnecessary internet exposure. Place NAS administration behind a VPN or dedicated management network and use firewall rules to limit connections to trusted administrators and systems.

Where possible, security teams should block direct inbound access to NAS management services from the internet. This does not replace the vendor patch because an attacker with access to the internal network could still target a vulnerable system, but it substantially reduces exposure to opportunistic scanning.

After applying the update, verify the installed DSM build rather than assuming an automatic-update notification confirms remediation. Synology notes that updates may become available at different times depending on region, model, and system configuration.

Devices running older DSM branches deserve additional attention. The technical advisory indicates that DSM versions before 6.2.4-25556-9 are affected, while modern remediation guidance centers primarily on supported 7.x releases. Organizations that cannot move an older appliance to a supported secure release should consider replacing, isolating, or removing that system from untrusted networks.

Security teams should also inspect systems that were publicly accessible before remediation. Review OAuth-related logs, administrative activity, file changes, service restarts, and unusual network events for evidence that exploitation attempts occurred before the update or workaround was applied.

Because arbitrary file writes are part of the confirmed impact, unexplained modification of configuration or application files should be treated more seriously than a normal failed authentication attempt. If suspicious file changes are identified, organizations should assess the NAS as potentially compromised rather than simply restoring the modified files.

Important data stored on NAS appliances should be protected by independent backups that attackers cannot modify through the same management plane. Maintaining offline, immutable, or separately authenticated backup copies can limit the operational impact of NAS compromise.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-120382 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-120382 is a critical argument-delimiter injection vulnerability in the OAuth API used by Synology DiskStation Manager. Improper neutralization of command arguments can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to influence a backend command and gain the ability to read or write arbitrary files or cause denial of service. Synology classifies the weakness as CWE-88 and assigns it a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

When was CVE-2026-120382 first discovered?

Synology has not publicly disclosed the original discovery date or named a researcher in the current advisory. The vulnerability became public on November 19, 2026, when Synology published Synology-SA-26:21. The advisory was last updated minutes after its initial publication and remains marked Ongoing while fixes for several affected branches are still being prepared.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-120382 on systems?

Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to read arbitrary files, write arbitrary files, and trigger denial-of-service conditions on affected Synology systems. This could expose sensitive NAS data, allow unauthorized modification of stored files, or disrupt services. Synology has not stated that the vulnerability directly provides arbitrary command execution or RCE.

Can CVE-2026-120382 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Systems running affected DSM builds or BeeStation OS 1.5 remain exposed until the appropriate security update is installed or the OAuth Service is deactivated. The advisory includes affected DSM branches from 6.2 through 7.4, although current support and patch availability differ by release.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-120382?

Install the relevant Synology security update as soon as it becomes available. DSM 7.4 systems should move to 7.4.1-90080-2 or later, while DSM 7.3 systems should move to 7.3.2-86009-6 or later. If the update is not yet available, deactivate the OAuth Service package, restrict NAS administration to trusted networks, and avoid exposing management interfaces directly to the internet.

items.title: Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers Delivering Malware
items.summary: A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers. The sites offer what they claim is a leaked or early Windows release of GTA 6. Instead of a playable game, the download delivers a ZIP archive containing a malicious program disguised as an installer. The campaign takes advantage of a familiar search: players looking for a GTA 6 PC release before they can get one through an official store. Earlier reporting on fake GTA 6 downloads documented a separate operation that bundled password stealers, remote-access malware and file-destroying code with a fake game installer. Those findings do not establish what CyberLeek’s launcher does after it runs. Researchers at the Vecert Foundation identified the malware distribution network and traced its activity to mid-October 2026, with notable spikes in November. The count comes from domain and certificate records. It reflects the size of the infrastructure the researchers linked to CyberLeek, not the number of people infected or the number of distinct malware samples. Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers One site examined by researchers advertised a playable GTA 6 port for Windows 10 and 11. It used search-friendly text and page markup that presented the supposed launcher as a software download. A prominent button promised a direct file with “no ad wall,” making the page look like a convenient alternative to the pop-ups and redirects users might expect from an unofficial download site. The download button did not always lead to the same file location. Researchers found that the page could send visitors to changing links on public hosting platforms, with a local ZIP archive available as a fallback. That distinction matters for defenders: blocking one download URL may leave the original landing page reachable and other download paths available. CyberLeek also used multiple domain endings and subdomains while keeping the same branding. This gave the campaign several places to send visitors if a site was blocked. Fake Launchger Node (Source – Vecert Foundation) The approach echoes gaming search poisoning campaigns that use credible-looking pages to reach people searching for game tools or popular software. A high search ranking does not verify who published a file or what it contains. The reported infection step is running the program inside the archive. Visiting the page or finding the ZIP in a Downloads folder does not, on its own, show that the installer ran. Fake GTA 6 demo In a separate case involving a fake GTA 6 demo , analysts identified Vidar, a program that steals passwords and browser sessions. Vecert did not name a specific malware family for CyberLeek or confirm what data the fake launcher collected. Security teams can search DNS and web proxy logs for the reported hosts, then compare any matches with endpoint records for archive downloads and installer launches. A generic script name or installer filename is not enough to establish a compromise. A recorded launch after a visit to a reported domain gives responders a stronger lead and a reason to check the device for unusual processes and network connections. Players who downloaded the ZIP but did not run it should delete it without opening the installer. Anyone who ran the program should disconnect the device from the network and have it checked. Since password and session theft can put accounts at risk even after the download is removed, use a clean device to change important passwords and revoke active sessions if compromise is suspected. For future releases, check the publisher’s official channels or a trusted storefront rather than a site promising an early build. items.title: The Sweet Spot Is a Day Old
items.summary: Every package we install brings someone else’s code into the environment we defend, along with all of its future updates. That raises a question we answer every day, usually without noticing: how new should the version we run be? Two risks On one side are old versions. Their bugs and vulnerabilities are known, documented and often exploited. They’re the ghosts of the past, and patching is how we escape them. Security teams push for faster updates, and they’re right to. On the other side is the release that went out an hour ago. It can contain new bugs, and sometimes it contains code that an attacker injected through a compromised maintainer account or build pipeline. Developers, organizations and users sit in between. They run from the old bugs straight into the risks of brand-new code. What a poisoned release does A malicious version doesn’t wait for a production deployment. It runs when a developer or a build job installs it. The payload in the TanStack compromise in May collected AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault, npm, GitHub and SSH credentials. The malicious Nx packages in August 2025 searched systems for sensitive data and uploaded the results to GitHub. Shai-Hulud used stolen npm tokens to publish infected versions of other packages its victims maintained. Build jobs are an attractive place for that code to run. They often hold credentials that reach much further than the build itself. Why a short wait works A malicious version only gets examined once it’s published and listed as the latest release. From that moment, researchers, security vendors such as Nextron and the community look at it. In my experience, most malicious versions are found within hours and nearly all within a day. The version is removed and the account that published it is blocked. The public timelines fit that observation. The axios versions that installed a remote access trojan in March were live for about three hours. In the TanStack case, an outside researcher reported the malicious versions within 26 minutes, and npm removed the last of them about four and a half hours after they were published. Last year, William Woodruff compiled ten prominent supply chain attacks. By his figures, seven of them had a window of opportunity of twelve hours or less. That suggests a simple rule: use the newest version once it has been public for at least a day. A day is the floor, not the ideal. Datadog’s security researchers describe a week as the common recommendation. In Woodruff’s list, the tj-actions compromise ran for about three days and the Kong Ingress Controller for about ten, so a longer wait catches more at the cost of slower updates. The newest version is the one nobody has looked at yet. The figures have limits. They only cover attacks that were caught. The xz-utils backdoor stayed in releases for about five weeks. The TanStack postmortem points out that the attacker’s code broke tests, and that a more careful attacker could have stayed hidden for hours longer. Once waiting becomes common, I expect attackers to delay their payloads too. A waiting period removes the fast, noisy attacks. It doesn’t replace lockfiles, scanning or short-lived credentials in build jobs. The cost: delayed security fixes A waiting period also delays the fix for a vulnerability that’s being exploited right now. That’s a real cost, and it needs an explicit answer. The update tools already have one. Dependabot’s cooldown applies to version updates, not to security updates. Renovate lets security updates bypass its minimumReleaseAge. pnpm audit --fix adds the patched version to pnpm's exclusion list, and npm audit fix warns when the waiting period blocks a fix. I'd handle it the same way: wait by default, give security releases a fast lane, and allow a manual override for a bug that's under active exploitation, with someone looking at the release before it goes in. Keep that exception narrow. An attacker who controls a maintainer account can call a release a security fix too. What’s supported today Most package managers added this over the past year, under different names and units: npm: min-release-age in days, since npm 11.10 pnpm: minimumReleaseAge in minutes, one day by default since pnpm 11 Yarn: npmMinimalAgeGate, as a duration such as 1w Bun: minimumReleaseAge in bunfig.toml, in seconds Deno: minimumDependencyAge, 24 hours by default since Deno 2.9 uv: exclude-newer, which accepts a relative duration such as 24 hours pip: --uploaded-prior-to, which accepts P1D since pip 26.1 Renovate: minimumReleaseAge Cargo: registry.global-min-publish-age, off by default Dependabot: cooldown, with three days by default for version updates Check the units. In pnpm, 1440 is one day. In Bun, it’s 24 minutes. There are gaps. Go’s proposal is on hold, and Andrew Nesbitt found no discussion of it at all for Maven, Gradle or Swift Package Manager. Every package manager, and browsers too I think every package manager should ship a minimum release age and turn it on by default, as pnpm and Deno now do. The same goes for anything else that installs third-party updates automatically. VS Code now waits two hours before it auto-updates an extension, and the delay is configurable. Browser extensions also update silently, can see everything a user does in the browser, and come from publishers whose accounts can be compromised like any maintainer’s. Chrome lets administrators pin an extension to a version, but I haven’t found a setting that delays updates. Browsers should add one. Cal Paterson goes a step further and proposes that registries hold new releases for a while before distributing them. That would also protect the people who never change a setting. Until then, the setting is ours to change, and a day is a good place to start. items.summary_html:
Every package we install brings someone else’s code into the environment we defend, along with all of its future updates. That raises a question we answer every day, usually without noticing: how new should the version we run be?

Two risks

On one side are old versions. Their bugs and vulnerabilities are known, documented and often exploited. They’re the ghosts of the past, and patching is how we escape them. Security teams push for faster updates, and they’re right to.

On the other side is the release that went out an hour ago. It can contain new bugs, and sometimes it contains code that an attacker injected through a compromised maintainer account or build pipeline.

Developers, organizations and users sit in between. They run from the old bugs straight into the risks of brand-new code.

What a poisoned release does

A malicious version doesn’t wait for a production deployment. It runs when a developer or a build job installs it. The payload in the TanStack compromise in May collected AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault, npm, GitHub and SSH credentials. The malicious Nx packages in August 2025 searched systems for sensitive data and uploaded the results to GitHub. Shai-Hulud used stolen npm tokens to publish infected versions of other packages its victims maintained.

Build jobs are an attractive place for that code to run. They often hold credentials that reach much further than the build itself.

Why a short wait works

A malicious version only gets examined once it’s published and listed as the latest release. From that moment, researchers, security vendors such as Nextron and the community look at it. In my experience, most malicious versions are found within hours and nearly all within a day. The version is removed and the account that published it is blocked.

The public timelines fit that observation. The axios versions that installed a remote access trojan in March were live for about three hours. In the TanStack case, an outside researcher reported the malicious versions within 26 minutes, and npm removed the last of them about four and a half hours after they were published. Last year, William Woodruff compiled ten prominent supply chain attacks. By his figures, seven of them had a window of opportunity of twelve hours or less.

That suggests a simple rule: use the newest version once it has been public for at least a day. A day is the floor, not the ideal. Datadog’s security researchers describe a week as the common recommendation. In Woodruff’s list, the tj-actions compromise ran for about three days and the Kong Ingress Controller for about ten, so a longer wait catches more at the cost of slower updates.

The newest version is the one nobody has looked at yet.

The figures have limits. They only cover attacks that were caught. The xz-utils backdoor stayed in releases for about five weeks. The TanStack postmortem points out that the attacker’s code broke tests, and that a more careful attacker could have stayed hidden for hours longer. Once waiting becomes common, I expect attackers to delay their payloads too. A waiting period removes the fast, noisy attacks. It doesn’t replace lockfiles, scanning or short-lived credentials in build jobs.

The cost: delayed security fixes

A waiting period also delays the fix for a vulnerability that’s being exploited right now. That’s a real cost, and it needs an explicit answer.

The update tools already have one. Dependabot’s cooldown applies to version updates, not to security updates. Renovate lets security updates bypass its minimumReleaseAge. pnpm audit --fix adds the patched version to pnpm's exclusion list, and npm audit fix warns when the waiting period blocks a fix. I'd handle it the same way: wait by default, give security releases a fast lane, and allow a manual override for a bug that's under active exploitation, with someone looking at the release before it goes in. Keep that exception narrow. An attacker who controls a maintainer account can call a release a security fix too.

What’s supported today

Most package managers added this over the past year, under different names and units:

  • npm: min-release-age in days, since npm 11.10
  • pnpm: minimumReleaseAge in minutes, one day by default since pnpm 11
  • Yarn: npmMinimalAgeGate, as a duration such as 1w
  • Bun: minimumReleaseAge in bunfig.toml, in seconds
  • Deno: minimumDependencyAge, 24 hours by default since Deno 2.9
  • uv: exclude-newer, which accepts a relative duration such as 24 hours
  • pip: --uploaded-prior-to, which accepts P1D since pip 26.1
  • Renovate: minimumReleaseAge
  • Cargo: registry.global-min-publish-age, off by default
  • Dependabot: cooldown, with three days by default for version updates

Check the units. In pnpm, 1440 is one day. In Bun, it’s 24 minutes.

There are gaps. Go’s proposal is on hold, and Andrew Nesbitt found no discussion of it at all for Maven, Gradle or Swift Package Manager.

Every package manager, and browsers too

I think every package manager should ship a minimum release age and turn it on by default, as pnpm and Deno now do. The same goes for anything else that installs third-party updates automatically. VS Code now waits two hours before it auto-updates an extension, and the delay is configurable. Browser extensions also update silently, can see everything a user does in the browser, and come from publishers whose accounts can be compromised like any maintainer’s. Chrome lets administrators pin an extension to a version, but I haven’t found a setting that delays updates. Browsers should add one.

Cal Paterson goes a step further and proposes that registries hold new releases for a while before distributing them. That would also protect the people who never change a setting. Until then, the setting is ours to change, and a day is a good place to start.

Further reading
  • William Woodruff, “We should all be using dependency cooldowns” and “Cooldowns redux”
  • Andrew Nesbitt, “Package managers need to cool down”
  • Datadog Security Labs, “The case for dependency cooldowns in a post-axios world”
  • Cal Paterson, “Dependency cooldowns turn you into a free-rider”

  • TanStack postmortem
  • Nx postmortem on the s1ngularity attack
  • Wiz on the chalk and debug compromise
  • Unit 42 on the Shai-Hulud worm

items.summary: .kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column491272_fbcef1-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article A ransomware group leaks files linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customers The data may include emails, phone numbers, and travel or dining bookings; no card numbers have been reported exposed Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing Customer information linked by researchers to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase has appeared after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. The companies report no impact to their payment networks. On November 19, the companies acknowledged incidents involving third-party providers. JPMorgan told Reuters : “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.” But “no payment data” doesn’t mean “not useful to criminals.” Knowing your name, email address and which financial services you use can give a scammer a convincing opening line. Visa said it was aware of the claims and that they were associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard said an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited number of email addresses associated with a particular card-benefit program. Cybernews researchers say similar formatting suggests the data came from the same third-party provider. The provider and its role haven’t been identified, but it may handle card benefits such as dining, reservations, or loyalty programs, rather than payment processing. The leaked records appear to relate to those extra services. A ransomware group calling itself n0n has claimed responsibility and published data it says it stole. What information was exposed? The answer depends on the company and on whether we are talking about company disclosures or researchers’ analysis of the purported stolen files. The leaked data has not been independently verified. Visa: An incident at an Asia-Pacific service provider. Visa says its systems were not affected and there is no indication that payment data, such as card numbers, was affected. In this article
  • A ransomware group leaks files linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customers
  • The data may include emails, phone numbers, and travel or dining bookings; no card numbers have been reported exposed
  • Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing

Customer information linked by researchers to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase has appeared after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. The companies report no impact to their payment networks.

On November 19, the companies acknowledged incidents involving third-party providers. JPMorgan told Reuters:

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

But “no payment data” doesn’t mean “not useful to criminals.” Knowing your name, email address and which financial services you use can give a scammer a convincing opening line.

Visa said it was aware of the claims and that they were associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard said an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited number of email addresses associated with a particular card-benefit program.

Cybernews researchers say similar formatting suggests the data came from the same third-party provider. The provider and its role haven’t been identified, but it may handle card benefits such as dining, reservations, or loyalty programs, rather than payment processing. The leaked records appear to relate to those extra services.

A ransomware group calling itself n0n has claimed responsibility and published data it says it stole.

What information was exposed?

The answer depends on the company and on whether we are talking about company disclosures or researchers’ analysis of the purported stolen files. The leaked data has not been independently verified.

The companies have disclosed the following:

  • JPMorgan Chase: Marketing data held by vendors, potentially including some customer names and email addresses.
  • Visa: An incident at an Asia-Pacific service provider. Visa says its systems were not affected and there is no indication that payment data, such as card numbers, was affected.
  • Mastercard: A limited number of email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. Mastercard described this as non-payment information.

The n0n leak site lists JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard and claims their data was published after the ransom deadline passed on November 16.

Screenshot of n0n leak site, November 20, 2026

Researchers at Cybernews reported additional details from the leaked datasets:

  • JPMorgan: Roughly 16,000 customer email addresses, some phone numbers, identifiers described as account IDs, and more than 100 employee email addresses.
  • Visa: A dataset involving more than 6,000 premium customers, with fields including names, email addresses, phone numbers, messaging-app information, and booking details such as dates and addresses.
  • Mastercard: Data posted by n0n includes marketing information related to customers in North America, the Middle East, and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses, according to Reuters.

If you’re concerned your information may be involved, these steps can help protect your accounts and identity:

  • Verify messages independently. Open your bank’s official app, use a website address you already know, or call the number on your card or statement. Do not use a link or phone number supplied by someone claiming to be investigating the breach.
  • Never read out a login or payment-verification code to an unexpected caller. Those codes can be the missing piece that allows a criminal to access your account. Enter them only when completing an action you initiated through the genuine service.
  • Do not transfer money to “protect” it. A caller who tells you to move your savings into a “safe account” is trying to steal them. Hang up and contact your bank independently.
  • Verify any offer of breach support before enrolling. JPMorgan says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.
  • Consider a credit freeze as a separate identity-protection measure.

items.title: Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool for Spying on Government Networks
items.summary: Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer of the traces defenders expect from a standard SoftEther installation. Researchers link the tool to Webworm, a China-aligned espionage group with a history of targeting government organizations, particularly in Europe. The distinction is that the bridge helps operators stay connected after a breach; the report does not show how they broke in. Nor does it name agencies newly affected by this build or establish what data, if any, was taken through it. Earlier coverage of Webworm’s GraphWorm documented a separate backdoor that used Microsoft OneDrive for communications. NtMonitor serves a different purpose: it gives operators a network route rather than a built-in command shell. Researchers from Rapid7 identified the modified VPN tool and attributed it to Webworm with moderate confidence in a November 19 report. They compared a public 64-bit Windows sample with the matching SoftEther source release, version 4.44, build 9807, and found no added command-execution backdoor. At the time of analysis, only one antivirus vendor on VirusTotal flagged the sample, even though it had been publicly available since January. Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool A VPN bridge connects networks rather than simply giving one user remote access. Every configuration Rapid7 examined linked a remote network to the local one. That can make the Windows host running the bridge a route to other systems on its network. The risk comes from an existing feature being used without authorization, not from a newly disclosed SoftEther vulnerability. Earlier reporting on Flax Typhoon’s SoftEther use illustrates how another group used the same open-source project to retain access after a breach. The public sample described itself as “Network Monitor Software” from “Network Systems Solutions Inc.” and listed netcapa.exe as its original filename. The disguise was inconsistent: some internal strings used NtMonitor branding, but the service entry point still referenced SEVPNBRIDGE , and several registry paths retained the SoftEther Project name. The build also packaged a normally separate resource archive inside the program and stored its settings in an encrypted file. Together, those changes meant an installation could look unfamiliar even to a team that knew what stock SoftEther leaves behind. The network traffic changed, too. Rapid7 found web request paths that resembled routine update traffic and a different marker in the opening exchange between VPN peers. That made signatures written for standard SoftEther traffic less useful. A separate case involving modified WireGuard also involved a rebuilt VPN tool, but that version ran embedded code. Rapid7 found no comparable execution feature in NtMonitor; the bridge itself was enough to maintain access. How Government Defenders Can Detect Unauthorized VPN Bridges Rapid7 found that configurations not considered likely tests pointed to addresses in AS20473, a hosting network associated with The Constant Company and Vultr. That overlap with past Webworm activity supported the attribution, but the network number alone is not evidence of compromise. ESET’s earlier Webworm research documented targeting in Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia, and Spain. Those countries describe earlier activity, not a confirmed victim list for NtMonitor. For defenders, the best starting point is an inventory of approved VPN services, the hosts allowed to run them, and the remote networks they are supposed to reach. Investigate unexpected Windows services, firewall rule changes, and connections to unapproved peers together. Earlier reporting on malware in isolated government networks illustrates why investigators should check which systems a compromised host could reach, not just identify the first machine that raised an alert. If a bridge is unauthorized, preserve its executable, configuration, and connection logs before removing it so responders can reconstruct where it led. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator type Source-reported value How to use it File hash prefix 90e7… Partial reference to the public sample; not a standalone match. Executable metadata netcapa.exe ; Network Monitor Software ; Network Systems Solutions Inc. Search file metadata and verify the binary’s provenance. Service and branding SEVPNBRIDGE ; NtMonitor VPN ; SoftEther Project Correlate with other findings; stock SoftEther can share some identifiers. Configuration setting.conf beginning with RCEN Check both the filename and the file header. HTTP paths /update/alive.cgi ; /update/picture.cgi Review alongside process and connection telemetry. Handshake signature POST /update/picture.cgi , Content-Type: image/jpeg , body starting 89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a 00 00 00 0d 49 48 44 52 Match the combined pattern where authorized TLS inspection provides visibility. Hosting infrastructure AS20473 Use as investigative context, not a blanket blocking rule. Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: OpenSSL Hit by Critical 9.8 Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability in Base64 Encoding Function
items.summary: A heap buffer overflow in OpenSSL’s Base64 encoding function can corrupt application memory when the library processes very large inputs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-121481, was published on November 18, 2026, with a critical CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8. That score describes the potential severity, but it does not mean every service that uses OpenSSL is remotely exposed. The flaw affects EVP_EncodeBlock() , which converts binary data into printable text. Base64 produces four output bytes for every three input bytes, with padding for a partial group. The application supplies the buffer that holds the result. For very large inputs, OpenSSL’s calculation of the encoded length can exceed the range of the integer used to store it. That calculation error can cause the encoder to write beyond the end of the supplied buffer. The write can corrupt nearby memory or crash the application. OpenSSL Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability This differs from the OpenSSL flaw that could leak server memory : the Base64 bug writes outside a buffer, while the earlier DTLS flaw read data outside one. The key question for security teams is whether an application passes large amounts of untrusted data to the affected encoder. A server’s use of OpenSSL for encrypted connections does not, by itself, answer that question. Teams should check where their applications call the function and which size limits apply before encoding begins. The CVE version record lists OpenSSL 4.0.0 through 4.0.3 and OpenSSL 4.1.0 as affected, with 4.0.4 and 4.1.1 marking the upper bounds of those ranges. OpenSSL branch Affected versions First fixed version 4.0.x 4.0.0 through 4.0.3, inclusive 4.0.4 4.1.x 4.1.0 4.1.1 3.x Outside the affected ranges in the upstream CVE record Not applicable Those version numbers do not, by themselves, confirm that a fixed package is available from a particular vendor. As with earlier OpenSSL memory corruption fixes , check the release or package notes for the branch you run. Ubuntu’s security tracker assigns the issue Medium priority and lists its main openssl packages as needing evaluation. It also marks the nodejs package in Ubuntu 22.04 LTS as vulnerable. Ubuntu notes that this package embeds its own copy of OpenSSL, so checking only the system library can miss software that bundles it. Inventory OpenSSL copies in system packages, containers, and application bundles. Prioritize applications that Base64-encode data supplied by users or external services. Until a vendor-confirmed update is available, enforce application-level input limits before encoding. After updating, restart or redeploy affected workloads and verify that they are running the updated build. For developers, the OpenSSL encoding documentation explains that callers must reserve space for the encoded data and a final zero byte that marks the end of the string. Review that calculation alongside input limits. For large files, consider an encoding interface that processes data in chunks rather than passing the whole file to one call. items.title: When a sync window closes: How Argo CD self-heal skipped the migration hook
items.summary: The uncomfortable question A few days ago, a customer asked me a question that sounded simple: “Argo CD said the sync succeeded, so why didn’t our migration run?” They had pushed a release while a deny sync window was active. When the window opened, five regional Applications rolled out the same commit. Three of them ran the database migration. Two did not, and the new code spent the next 36 to 44 minutes talking to a schema it did not understand. My first instinct was to blame something specific to their setup. I was wrong. It took me two days, a throwaway lab, and a careful read of the Argo CD source to see that this is not bad luck. It is a race, and with the right timing, anyone can lose it. Synced, healthy, and wrong What bothered me most was how normal everything looked. The two broken Applications were Synced and Healthy on the new commit. Their last operation said “successfully synced (all tasks run)”. If you only looked at the UI, you would have signed off on the release. The setup itself was ordinary. One service, five regions, one Application per region, automated sync with prune and self-heal turned on. Production sat behind a deny window outside business hours, and the migration ran as a Sync hook Job, which is exactly how many of us were taught to do it. The only clue was buried in the controller log. The two bad operations listed thirteen specific resources and carried a self-heal attempt count of one. In other words, Argo CD had not deployed a release. It had healed drift, and healing drift never runs hooks. A lab you can break on purpose I don’t trust an explanation until I can make the failure happen on demand, so I built the smallest setup I could. The app was as plain as I could make it. One Application with automated sync, prune, and self-heal. A ConfigMap and a Deployment that carry a release string, so every release makes the app OutOfSync. And a migration that runs as a Sync hook, labelled with its release so I could see at a glance which one last ran: apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata: name: db-migration labels: release: "v11" annotations: argocd.argoproj.io/hook: Sync argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation spec: backoffLimit: 0 template: spec: restartPolicy: Never containers: - name: migrate image: busybox:1.36 command: ["sh", "-c", "echo migrating schema to v11; sleep 3"] The last piece was a deny window on the project, four minutes long and starting at the current minute, so I knew to the second when it would close. My first attempt did not reproduce anything, and that turned out to be the most useful run of the day. The app’s periodic refresh landed in the same second as my trigger, won the race, and did a perfectly correct full sync. So I changed the script. I pushed release v11 while the window was active , and refreshed the app fifteen seconds before the close to push its next periodic refresh a couple of minutes out. The app synced v11 in one second, and the UI looked spotless. Then I opened the migration Job. It still said release: v10. I reproduced it five times out of six. The failure was not rare. It only needed the wrong event to arrive first. The first refresh wins With debug logging on, the story was right there. Argo CD refreshes an Application for two very different reasons. A level-2 refresh comes from the reconciliation timer, roughly every two to three minutes, and compares the app against Git. A level-1 refresh comes from a change to a managed object and reuses what the controller already knows. When a window closes, nothing announces it. The next refresh of either kind simply finds that syncing is allowed again, and whichever kind arrives first decides what happens next. During the window, the timer-driven refreshes keep comparing the new commit and record it in status.sync.revision , while the last real sync stays on the old commit. A level-1 refresh then uses that same recorded revision as the one to compare, checks it against itself in evaluateRevisionChanges , and concludes there are no changes. With no changes, alreadyAttemptedSyn c only compares the Application’s source, which has not changed either, so the controller decides it already synced this revision. With self-heal on, that means healing drift: a sync of only the out-of-sync resources, which is a partial sync, which skips hooks and writes no history. A timer-driven refresh compares against targetRevision instead, notices that the last synced revision is older, and runs a normal full sync with hooks. The bug fits in one sentence. On the level-1 path, the last compared revision is mistaken for the last synced one. A hook is not a guarantee It is tempting to reach for a quick fix inside the hook model. Make the migration a PreSync hook instead of a Sync hook. Turn on the newer RunHooksOnPartialSync option. Shorten the window. From what I read in the code, none of these change the outcome. A partial sync skips every hook type, the new option is ignored for automated syncs, and self-heal is automated by definition. The race happens at every window close, whatever its length. I didn’t test these three, but the code leaves little room for doubt. The real lesson is broader than this bug. A hook runs when a particular kind of operation runs. If the release can reach the cluster through any other kind of operation, the hook is a hope, not a guarantee. Make the migration part of the desired state The fix I now recommend is to stop treating the migration as a side effect of syncing and make it part of what gets synced. Remove the hook annotations, give the Job a sync wave that runs before the app, and give it a name that changes every release. apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata: name: db-migration-v11 # change per release annotations: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1" Now the migration is an ordinary managed resource. A new release brings a Job that does not exist yet, so any sync, partial or full, sees it as missing and applies it, and Argo CD waits for that wave to be healthy before it touches the next one. In my lab, the wave version went through the exact broken self-heal path, and the migration still finished, one second before the new ConfigMap and Deployment were applied. The previous release’s Job was pruned on the way. There are a few details worth getting right. Use a unique name per release, such as the image tag in a Helm template, because a Job’s pod template is immutable. Keep prune on so old Jobs are cleaned up. Don’t set ttlSecondsAfterFinished , or Kubernetes will delete the Job, self-heal will see a missing resource, and your migration will run again. Keep migrations idempotent anyway. And try a deliberately failing migration in staging before you rely on this, because that is the one case I did not test. Or let the timer decide If changing every chart is not an option this week, there is a blunter tool. Turn off self-heal on the apps that run migrations. syncPolicy: automated: prune: true selfHeal: false I ran two apps through the same window to compare. Both made the same faulty “no changes” decision. The one with self-heal on deployed v11 without its migration. The one with self-heal off logged “Skipping auto-sync: most recent sync already to […]” and simply waited. About two minutes later, its timer-driven refresh compared against the real last sync and ran a full sync with the hook, and the v11 migration finished. No manual sync, and no window of mismatched code and schema, because the app stayed entirely on the old release while it waited. The price is drift correction. Anyone who edits a resource by hand now leaves it OutOfSync until the next commit. Trust the sync, not the timing Sync windows, self-heal, and hooks are each reasonable on their own. Together they leave a gap that opens at every window close, and whether you fall into it depends on which event reaches the controller first. I don’t think you should have to win a race to get a correct release. So I stopped letting a hook be the only thing that runs a migration. If the schema change is part of the desired state, every path that syncs the release also syncs the migration. We do not need to trust the timing. We need to trust what we put in Git. References Argo CD docs: Sync Windows Argo CD docs: Resource Hooks Argo CD docs: Sync Phases and Waves

Synced, healthy, and wrong

What bothered me most was how normal everything looked. The two broken Applications were Synced and Healthy on the new commit. Their last operation said “successfully synced (all tasks run)”. If you only looked at the UI, you would have signed off on the release.

The setup itself was ordinary. One service, five regions, one Application per region, automated sync with prune and self-heal turned on. Production sat behind a deny window outside business hours, and the migration ran as a Sync hook Job, which is exactly how many of us were taught to do it.

The only clue was buried in the controller log. The two bad operations listed thirteen specific resources and carried a self-heal attempt count of one. In other words, Argo CD had not deployed a release. It had healed drift, and healing drift never runs hooks.

A lab you can break on purpose

I don’t trust an explanation until I can make the failure happen on demand, so I built the smallest setup I could.

The app was as plain as I could make it. One Application with automated sync, prune, and self-heal. A ConfigMap and a Deployment that carry a release string, so every release makes the app OutOfSync. And a migration that runs as a Sync hook, labelled with its release so I could see at a glance which one last ran:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migration
  labels:
    release: "v11"
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: Sync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo migrating schema to v11; sleep 3"]

The last piece was a deny window on the project, four minutes long and starting at the current minute, so I knew to the second when it would close.

My first attempt did not reproduce anything, and that turned out to be the most useful run of the day. The app’s periodic refresh landed in the same second as my trigger, won the race, and did a perfectly correct full sync. So I changed the script. I pushed release v11 while the window was active, and refreshed the app fifteen seconds before the close to push its next periodic refresh a couple of minutes out.

The app synced v11 in one second, and the UI looked spotless.

Then I opened the migration Job. It still said release: v10.

I reproduced it five times out of six. The failure was not rare. It only needed the wrong event to arrive first.

The first refresh wins

With debug logging on, the story was right there. Argo CD refreshes an Application for two very different reasons. A level-2 refresh comes from the reconciliation timer, roughly every two to three minutes, and compares the app against Git. A level-1 refresh comes from a change to a managed object and reuses what the controller already knows. When a window closes, nothing announces it. The next refresh of either kind simply finds that syncing is allowed again, and whichever kind arrives first decides what happens next.

During the window, the timer-driven refreshes keep comparing the new commit and record it in status.sync.revision, while the last real sync stays on the old commit. A level-1 refresh then uses that same recorded revision as the one to compare, checks it against itself in evaluateRevisionChanges, and concludes there are no changes. With no changes, alreadyAttemptedSync only compares the Application’s source, which has not changed either, so the controller decides it already synced this revision. With self-heal on, that means healing drift: a sync of only the out-of-sync resources, which is a partial sync, which skips hooks and writes no history.

A timer-driven refresh compares against targetRevision instead, notices that the last synced revision is older, and runs a normal full sync with hooks. The bug fits in one sentence. On the level-1 path, the last compared revision is mistaken for the last synced one.

A hook is not a guarantee

It is tempting to reach for a quick fix inside the hook model. Make the migration a PreSync hook instead of a Sync hook. Turn on the newer RunHooksOnPartialSync option. Shorten the window. From what I read in the code, none of these change the outcome. A partial sync skips every hook type, the new option is ignored for automated syncs, and self-heal is automated by definition. The race happens at every window close, whatever its length. I didn’t test these three, but the code leaves little room for doubt.

The real lesson is broader than this bug. A hook runs when a particular kind of operation runs. If the release can reach the cluster through any other kind of operation, the hook is a hope, not a guarantee.

Make the migration part of the desired state

The fix I now recommend is to stop treating the migration as a side effect of syncing and make it part of what gets synced. Remove the hook annotations, give the Job a sync wave that runs before the app, and give it a name that changes every release.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migration-v11            # change per release
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"

Now the migration is an ordinary managed resource. A new release brings a Job that does not exist yet, so any sync, partial or full, sees it as missing and applies it, and Argo CD waits for that wave to be healthy before it touches the next one. In my lab, the wave version went through the exact broken self-heal path, and the migration still finished, one second before the new ConfigMap and Deployment were applied. The previous release’s Job was pruned on the way.

There are a few details worth getting right. Use a unique name per release, such as the image tag in a Helm template, because a Job’s pod template is immutable. Keep prune on so old Jobs are cleaned up. Don’t set ttlSecondsAfterFinished, or Kubernetes will delete the Job, self-heal will see a missing resource, and your migration will run again. Keep migrations idempotent anyway. And try a deliberately failing migration in staging before you rely on this, because that is the one case I did not test.

Or let the timer decide

If changing every chart is not an option this week, there is a blunter tool. Turn off self-heal on the apps that run migrations.

syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: false

I ran two apps through the same window to compare. Both made the same faulty “no changes” decision. The one with self-heal on deployed v11 without its migration. The one with self-heal off logged “Skipping auto-sync: most recent sync already to […]” and simply waited. About two minutes later, its timer-driven refresh compared against the real last sync and ran a full sync with the hook, and the v11 migration finished.

No manual sync, and no window of mismatched code and schema, because the app stayed entirely on the old release while it waited. The price is drift correction. Anyone who edits a resource by hand now leaves it OutOfSync until the next commit.

Trust the sync, not the timing

Sync windows, self-heal, and hooks are each reasonable on their own. Together they leave a gap that opens at every window close, and whether you fall into it depends on which event reaches the controller first. I don’t think you should have to win a race to get a correct release.

So I stopped letting a hook be the only thing that runs a migration. If the schema change is part of the desired state, every path that syncs the release also syncs the migration. We do not need to trust the timing. We need to trust what we put in Git.

References
  • Argo CD docs: Sync Windows
  • Argo CD docs: Resource Hooks
  • Argo CD docs: Sync Phases and Waves

items.title: BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers Across Hospitals and Universities
items.summary: Staff at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center reported hearing ransom messages from their computers during an October 26 cyberattack. Two weeks later, a recording from Vanderbilt University captured a voice announcing, “You have been compromised by BYOD.” The messages took the ransom demand out of a private note and made the incident visible to people far beyond the IT team. The disruptions were real, even where the hackers’ claims remain unverified. New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center diverted ambulances for two hours, and more than 30 clinics canceled appointments and outpatient surgeries. On November 9, Vanderbilt told students, faculty and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi while it investigated. Researchers at TrendAI noted the reported ransomware activity in their analysis of the BYOD campaign, which claimed at least nine organizations between October 5 and November 9, 2026. The researchers did not have a public malware sample to examine. Their findings draw on victim statements, public reporting and claims by the group, so the report separates confirmed disruptions from unverified accounts of encryption and data theft. BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers At UNM, employees reported that the audio claimed patient, student and employee data had been stolen. BYOD later claimed it compromised 36,000 systems, including Microsoft Entra and two Oracle databases. UNM said the incident affected some end-user devices but did not reach core systems or servers. As the Ascension hospital ransomware incident also showed, ambulance diversion is an operational consequence, not a measure of how far attackers reached. The Vanderbilt campus device shutdown came as the university warned users about unfamiliar applications, unexpected login approval requests and unusual file or permission changes. Campus Wi-Fi returned that evening, with other services restored in phases. BYOD claimed it encrypted databases and stole more than one million Social Security numbers, but Vanderbilt had not confirmed the group’s involvement, encryption or data theft in the reporting reviewed by TrendAI. The audio tells investigators less than it might seem. It shows that a message played on affected computers, but it does not establish how the group delivered it, whether the same method was used at both sites, or whether attackers controlled a central directory. Its clearest effect was public pressure: staff and students could hear and record the demand before either institution had finished assessing the incident. Credential compromise Michigan State University offers a separate clue about account security. It reported a possible credential compromise and required university password resets in early October, before BYOD listed it on November 1. The university said it had no evidence that its central Active Directory was compromised or that other data was accessed, altered or stolen. The group’s claim about 1.3 million current and former students therefore remains unverified. Unexpected login prompts deserve attention even when endpoint tools find no malware. Separate reporting on cloud account takeover tactics shows how repeated approval requests can precede unauthorized access. TrendAI recommends checking identity, endpoint and cloud logs together, then reviewing what a suspected account accessed before its password was reset, including shared files and administrative settings. For hospitals, the response plan should also cover what happens when staff cannot use their computers. TrendAI advises testing offline backups and rehearsing downtime procedures that do not depend on the network. The company also recommends giving patients, students and staff a trusted way to report unsolicited messages from anyone claiming to hold their data. That preparation matters before the first ransom message plays, because restoring computers and containing public pressure are two different jobs.
